The second, is the random objectives in the bottom left that you are pretty much forced to do if you want as many points as possible and if they don't roll the ones that benefit you, you'll waste a lot of points. Do you like 'number go up'? Do you like skill trees? Do you like minimalism themed around squares? Do you like strategy-focused idler games that fully play themselves, where you only have to check in occasionally and click a few things to make number go up again and then check back out? This game is for you! This game boasts an infinite skill tree, and the way they keep that from getting out of hand is with two currency types, one gained linearly and one gained logrithimically. The skill tree expands from a combination of both types, so at some point, progress grinds to a halt for hours, nudging you to do a prestige and reset everything back to 1, with persistent upgrades to make progress go faster. With time, I'm sure some dedicated players will push the skill tree to the limits of their CPUs and we'll surely see some mind-boggling screenshots to prove it! There is an optional mechanic of 'quests' which pop up in the bottom left, and you can simply minimize and ignore them. You get 3 options and can only complete one, then the list refreshes. The quests can guide you to min-max one stat specifically for a while, so you get to really see the impact it has on the gameplay. i came to really appreciate multi-shot from that! Has that soothing effect of watching all your problems burst away... And when they get too big? You may be defeated, but you'll come back stronger and blow right past them the next time you meet.

I like it, it's polished and looks good. My main issue is having to spend massive amounts of points to level up which wave you get knocked back to when you die. You can spend tons of diamonds and still get knocked back over 100 levels. Wave upgrades should not scale the way they do. Getting knocked back so many levels just creates tedium and waiting around, which (conveniently?) pads playtime. Way too much waiting around to get back up to having a chance to beat your previous best wave. Nonetheless, I'm still having fun and don't think this deserves a negative review.

I originally was going to recommend this game, but then saw it was on a discount currently, it's full price is 4.29 pounds (Just short of six dollars) I feel that's too much for a game you're literally not going to be playing, it's just going to be sitting in another tab. Not a very exciting idle game. It's something to occupy a second screen or another tab. You check back now and then and click the talent tree. It's fun to click the talent tree and get more abilities to make the dots shoot better.... But it's not a game to be played actively. You'll be bored out of your skull. If you have any kind of colour blindness, every colour in this game is extremely similar to each other, some people have noted issues seeing the skill tree. Hopefully the devs add colour change options. You can turn off post process and screenshake, so the game looks less like a migraine aura. Another commenter mentions that the game runs poorly. I personally have had no issues with it, it uses a gig of memory in the task manager. My fans are chillin', just happy, sat not really paying attention. Given we're going through a heatwave, it's a surprise they're not already suffering. But I do have a LOT of cooling. So I don't know. They were using AMD, I have Nvidia. The dev says they've fixed an issue with AMD. So maybe that's the problem sorted. It's not a terrible game, it's just not terribly exciting. I'd say you should only get it if you don't want to actively play it. Which sounds like a contradiction, but think of it like an idle game. Thanks for reading, or skipping to the end. Whether or not you agree with me, I hope you have a lovely day. I hope I get to click recommended on a game some day....

Incremental Infinity is an idle game that fully commits to the appeal of endless progression. Developed and published by Rablo Games, it places players in a minimalist universe where every action contributes to one goal: becoming unimaginably powerful. Rather than hiding its intentions behind an elaborate story or flashy presentation, the game embraces the fundamentals of the incremental genre. You begin with little more than a single point of power and slowly climb toward astronomical values, watching your influence expand with every upgrade, reset, and ascension. It is a straightforward concept, but one that proves surprisingly difficult to put down once the progression systems begin to overlap. At the center of the experience is a procedurally generated skill tree that serves as both the game's greatest strength and its defining feature. Every playthrough presents a fresh arrangement of upgrades, encouraging experimentation instead of rigid optimization. New sectors continuously unlock, revealing additional paths that enhance combat efficiency, resource gain, and overall progression speed. Supplementing this are quests and upgrade pools that introduce further opportunities for specialization. The result is a gameplay loop that feels dynamic despite its relatively simple foundation, as players are constantly deciding where to invest their growing resources. Combat is intentionally passive, with your character automatically attacking waves of numbered enemies that steadily increase in difficulty. While the action itself is uncomplicated, the satisfaction comes from witnessing the dramatic escalation of your capabilities. One particularly clever mechanic ties your numerical value directly to your character's size and durability. As your number rises, so does your presence on the battlefield, creating a visible representation of your advancement. It is a small detail, but it helps reinforce the game's central theme of infinite growth in a meaningful way. Death is not treated as a punishment so much as an expected part of the journey. Losing a run resets your value to its starting point, yet permanent upgrades remain, ensuring that every setback contributes to future progress. This roguelite-inspired structure keeps the gameplay engaging over extended sessions, as each attempt becomes an opportunity to push a little farther than before. The ascension system strengthens this approach by rewarding players with lasting bonuses and increased experience gains, creating a satisfying cycle of rebuilding and optimization that genre fans will immediately recognize. Incremental Infinity also excels as a secondary game. Its low-maintenance design makes it ideal for running in the background while working, browsing the internet, or playing another title. The interface is generally clean and accessible during the early hours, and the minimalist visuals ensure that information remains easy to read. However, the game's ambition occasionally works against it. As the skill tree expands into a massive web of interconnected upgrades, navigation can become cumbersome. Locating specific nodes or planning long-term routes becomes increasingly difficult, and additional organizational tools would significantly improve the overall experience. Despite these shortcomings, Rablo Games has created a compelling package for fans of idle and incremental titles. The game understands its audience and rarely strays from what makes the genre enjoyable. Players looking for narrative depth, complex mechanics, or active gameplay may struggle to remain invested, but those who enjoy watching numbers climb into absurd territory will likely find themselves captivated. Incremental Infinity succeeds because it remains focused on its core philosophy from beginning to end: every reset matters, every upgrade counts, and there is always another milestone waiting just beyond the horizon. Rating: 6/10

This incremental has tons of potential, even if it's still a little rough around the edges. I genuinely love it. The idea of a procedurally generated skill tree is awesome and keeps every run feeling fresh, although it can be a bit frustrating since luck plays such a big role. I think it'd be great if you could pick a couple of guaranteed starting skills before each run to reduce some of the RNG. The progression is a bit of a mixed bag for me. Seeing the numbers go up and surviving bigger and bigger waves scratches that incremental itch perfectly. However, I'd love to see an Ascension upgrade that increases the number of skill points you earn each run, similar to the existing upgrade that boosts diamond gains. I think that would make the early and mid-game progression feel much smoother. I'd also love to see some sort of Challenge Mode: separate runs where you start from scratch with special restrictions or objectives, and completing them rewards your main save with permanent bonuses. That would add a lot of replayability. An Ultra Ascension mechanic could also be really fun, offering an even bigger reset with stronger permanent upgrades. I know that would probably be difficult to balance, but it would make for an exciting late-game goal. And of course, more weapons, skills, and build variety are always welcome, but I'm sure those will come with future updates. Overall, this is an incredibly fun incremental that already has a really solid foundation. With a few updates and some extra content, I can easily see it becoming one of the best games in the genre. Absolutely GOATED.

The devs are trying to make changes, including nerfing damage because the one thing to make it less of a grind was apparently a nono, so now you need to play on "easy" mode to get old value, but are there any redeming values in the gameplay loop right now? no, even as a "number go bigger game" no, someone said they wish it could just auto assign points at random, which would remove the tiny amount of interaction but i would agree, atleast then you can see numbers get bigger without needing to check it and click a handful of times every 15 minutes because thats all the gameplay amounts to.
